questions.question: What are the base case and recursive case in recursion?
questions.title: Base cases and progress in recursion
questions.direct_answer: The base case returns without another recursive call, while the recursive case reduces the problem and calls the function again. Correct recursion must move toward a reachable base case on every path.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: The base case stops new calls.
The recursive case solves a smaller problem.
Every path must make measurable progress.
Each unfinished call stays on the call stack.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Recursion is a function solving a problem by calling itself with a smaller version. The base case handles the smallest result directly and stops the chain. The recursive case reduces the input, delegates the smaller work, and combines that result.

For example, factorial uses `factorial(0) = 1` as its base case. For a positive n, it returns `n * factorial(n - 1)`. Calling `factorial(3)` creates `3 * factorial(2)`, then `2 * factorial(1)`, before the base result lets the calls return.

A recursive function fails when the base case is missing, cannot be reached, or some branch does not make progress. JavaScript also has a finite call stack, so very deep valid recursion can still throw a range error. Iteration is often safer for a simple long linear sequence.

sections.title: Termination, progress, and pending work
sections.content:
A termination argument names a measure that becomes smaller, such as `n`, the remaining array length, or the height below a tree node. The base case covers the minimum measure, and every recursive call moves toward it.

The statements after a recursive call are pending until the smaller call returns. This unwind phase is useful for tree results and reversed order, but it also explains the memory cost: each unfinished call needs a stack frame.

sections.title: Recursive call and return path
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[factorial 3] --> B[factorial 2]
  B --> C[factorial 1]
  C --> D[factorial 0 = 1]
  D --> E[return 1]
  E --> F[return 2]
  F --> G[return 6]
```

questions.question: How do you calculate factorial recursively in JavaScript?
questions.title: Recursive factorial with input boundaries
questions.direct_answer: Return 1 for zero, otherwise return `n * factorial(n - 1)`. Validate that n is a non-negative integer, and remember that JavaScript Number loses integer precision for large factorials.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Reduce n by one each call.
Reject negative and non-integer input.
Large results exceed Number's safe integer range.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Factorial multiplies every positive integer from n down to one. The recursive definition is `0! = 1` and `n! = n × (n - 1)!`, so the JavaScript function can follow the mathematical rule directly.

For example, `factorial(4)` becomes `4 * factorial(3)`, then `4 * 3 * factorial(2)`, and finally returns `24` after reaching zero. Each call waits for the smaller result before multiplying.

The algorithm performs O(n) multiplications and uses O(n) call-stack space. It should reject negative or fractional inputs. JavaScript Number stops representing every integer exactly above `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`, so larger exact results need `BigInt` and an `n` suffix-compatible implementation.

sections.title: The factorial recurrence and numeric limits
sections.content:
The base value must be one because it is the multiplicative identity and makes `1! = 1 × 0!` correct. Returning zero at the base would make every factorial zero.

An iterative loop has the same O(n) time and only O(1) call-stack space. Recursion is useful here for learning the recurrence, but iteration is usually the practical choice when n may be large enough to threaten stack depth.

questions.question: How do you reverse a string using recursion?
questions.title: Recursive string reversal
questions.direct_answer: Return the string when it has at most one unit; otherwise reverse the remainder and append the first unit. Convert with `[...text]` first when the interview expects Unicode code points rather than UTF-16 code units.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Length zero or one is the base case.
The recursive input must become smaller.
Append the removed first item during unwinding.
String slicing can make the simple version O(n²).

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Recursive reversal removes one character, reverses the rest, and places the removed character at the end. The base case is an empty string or one character, which is already reversed.

For example, reversing `cat` becomes `reverse('at') + 'c'`, then `reverse('t') + 'a' + 'c'`, and returns `tac` as the calls unwind. The output order is created after each smaller call returns.

The idea visits n units, but repeated slicing and string concatenation can copy growing strings and make a simple JavaScript version O(n²). An array plus two-pointer swap is more practical. Also, direct string indexing uses UTF-16 code units; `[...text]` handles code points better but still does not combine every user-perceived grapheme.

sections.title: Unwinding builds the reversed order
sections.content:
The recursive call delays the first character until the suffix has been reversed. That pending append is why the order changes during the return path rather than during the descent.

A range-based helper can avoid creating a new substring at every call, but it still uses O(n) stack frames. For production text, an iterative array reversal is clearer and avoids stack overflow on long input.

questions.question: How do you trace the call stack of a recursive function?
questions.title: Tracing recursive calls and returns
questions.direct_answer: Write each call's argument while recursion descends, mark the base result, then work upward in reverse order and calculate every return value. Each row represents one pending stack frame.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Record the argument for every call.
Stop at the exact base case.
Return in reverse call order.
Include local values used after the recursive call.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A recursion trace has two directions: calls go down toward the base case, and results come back up. Each unfinished call keeps its argument and local variables in a stack frame until the smaller call returns.

For example, `sum(3)` may return `3 + sum(2)`, so the stack holds pending additions for 3, 2, and 1. The base `sum(0)` returns 0; unwinding then returns 1, 3, and finally 6.

A useful trace table has columns for depth, call argument, pending operation, and returned value. It exposes off-by-one base cases and branches that fail to reduce the input. For tree recursion, draw both child calls before calculating the parent result because the stack follows depth-first order.

sections.title: Stack frames preserve unfinished calculations
sections.content:
The call stack is last-in, first-out. For example, `sum(0)` returns before the pending `sum(1)`, `sum(2)`, and `sum(3)` frames can finish, so results are completed in the opposite order from the calls.

Logging only on entry shows the descent but hides the result flow. Logging both before and after the recursive call makes the two phases visible and helps distinguish a wrong recursive input from a wrong combination step.

sections.title: Trace of sum(3)
sections.content:
| Depth | Call | Pending work | Return |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | sum(3) | 3 + sum(2) | 6 |
| 1 | sum(2) | 2 + sum(1) | 3 |
| 2 | sum(1) | 1 + sum(0) | 1 |
| 3 | sum(0) | base case | 0 |

questions.question: When is iteration safer than recursion in JavaScript?
questions.title: Recursion versus iteration in JavaScript
questions.direct_answer: Iteration is safer for very deep linear work because it does not create one JavaScript call frame per step. Recursion remains clear for naturally nested data when depth is controlled or an explicit stack would only repeat the same structure.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Deep recursion can overflow the call stack.
Loops use constant call-stack space.
Trees often match recursive structure naturally.
An explicit stack keeps depth under program control.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Iteration is usually safer when the problem may require thousands of simple sequential steps. A recursive call normally adds a stack frame, and JavaScript engines do not generally guarantee tail-call optimization for ordinary deployed code.

For example, walking a linked list with one million nodes recursively can exceed the call stack even though the algorithm is logically correct. A `while` loop keeps only the current node. A small balanced tree, however, is often clearer as a recursive depth-first traversal.

Both forms can have the same time complexity. The difference is control flow and auxiliary storage: recursion uses the language call stack, while an iterative depth-first search can use an explicit array stack. Choose recursion when the nested definition improves clarity and maximum depth is safe; otherwise use a loop or explicit work list.

sections.title: Call-stack depth is an input constraint
sections.content:
Big O alone does not capture the runtime limit. For example, O(n) recursive and iterative linked-list traversals may perform similar work, but only the recursive version depends on the engine's maximum call depth.

An explicit stack does not always reduce O(n) auxiliary space for a tree traversal, but it moves storage to the heap and lets the program pause, inspect, or limit the work instead of risking an implicit call-stack failure.

sections.title: Recursive and iterative traversal
sections.content:
| Concern | Recursion | Iteration or explicit stack |
|---|---|---|
| Code shape | Matches nested definitions | Makes control flow explicit |
| Very deep input | May overflow call stack | Can continue within heap limits |
| Stored work | Call frames | Loop variables or array stack |
| Best fit | Controlled trees and divide-and-conquer | Long linear or depth-unknown work |
